passages.t: Futility of futilities, and nothing new under the sun
passages.happening:
‘These are the words of the Teacher, the son of David, king in Jerusalem’ (verse 1). Then comes the motto of the whole book: “Futility of futilities,” says the Teacher, “futility of futilities! Everything is futile!” (verse 2).

The question that drives the book follows at once: ‘What does a man gain from all his labor, at which he toils under the sun?’ (verse 3).

A poem answers with pictures of endless motion. ‘Generations come and generations go, but the earth remains forever’ (verse 4). The sun rises and sets and hurries back to rise again (verse 5). The wind goes round and round (verse 6). ‘All the rivers flow into the sea, yet the sea is never full’ (verse 7). ‘All things are wearisome, more than one can describe; the eye is not satisfied with seeing, nor the ear content with hearing’ (verse 8).

‘What has been will be again, and what has been done will be done again; there is nothing new under the sun’ (verse 9). And no one is remembered: ‘There is no remembrance of those who came before’ (verse 11).
passages.hearers:
The first two verses are spoken by a narrator, who talks about the Teacher instead of as the Teacher. That narrator will return at the book's end (12:8-14) and frame everything in between.

The key word, hevel, means breath or vapor, the mist of breath on a cold morning. The BSB translates it futile, others vanity, meaningless or fleeting. Futility of futilities is a Hebrew way of saying the utmost, the way the holy of holies means the most holy place.

Gain, yitron, is a word found in the Old Testament only in Ecclesiastes. It sounds like the language of business: what is left over at the end, the profit. The Teacher asks what profit a whole life of labor leaves.

The pictures in verses 4 to 7 come from the world as ancient people saw it. The sun was pictured hurrying back each night to its place of rising. Rivers ran into the sea and never filled it. The poem is not a science lesson. Its rhythm copies what it describes, going and coming, round and round, motion that never arrives anywhere new. This is the world after Genesis 3, where work has become toil and every generation returns to the dust.
passages.later: The psalms say the same of human life: ‘Man is like a breath; his days are like a passing shadow’ (Psalm 144:4). And Paul takes up the book's word when he writes that ‘the creation was subjected to futility’, and adds that it was ‘in hope’ (Romans 8:20).
passages.hard:
Is the Bible saying that life is meaningless?

Read on its own, verse 2 can sound like despair. But the key word, hevel, has a range of meanings.

Some interpreters take it as meaningless or empty, and read the Teacher's words as an honest portrait of life without God, which the book's frame then corrects. Others read hevel as brevity: life is a breath, short and fragile, not worthless but passing. Still others take it as enigma: life cannot be figured out or mastered.

The phrase under the sun (verse 3) also matters. The Teacher is describing life as seen from inside the world's own resources, and the book's narrator will close by pointing to the fear of God and his coming judgment (12:13-14). Most readers agree that the Bible is not saying God's world or human life has no worth. It is saying that nothing under the sun can give the lasting gain people seek from it.
passages.asks: The Teacher asks what all your labor gains. Ask what you are working for, and whether it can bear the weight you are putting on it. And ask where in the ordinary turning of days you have stopped expecting anything new from God.

passages.t: A king's search, and much wisdom, much sorrow
passages.happening:
Now the Teacher speaks for himself. ‘I, the Teacher, was king over Israel in Jerusalem’ (verse 12). He set his mind to explore by wisdom everything done under heaven. ‘What a heavy burden God has laid upon the sons of men to occupy them’ (verse 13).

‘I have seen all the things that are done under the sun, and have found them all to be futile, a pursuit of the wind’ (verse 14). ‘What is crooked cannot be straightened, and what is lacking cannot be counted’ (verse 15).

He grew in wisdom beyond all who had been over Jerusalem before him (verse 16). He set his mind to know wisdom, and madness and folly too, ‘I learned that this, too, is a pursuit of the wind’ (verse 17). The chapter ends with a two-line proverb: ‘For with much wisdom comes much sorrow, and as knowledge grows, grief increases’ (verse 18).
passages.hearers:
The Teacher presents himself as the person best placed to search for an answer: a king, with every resource and a mind full of wisdom. Tradition identified him with Solomon, who reigned in the tenth century BC and was famed for wisdom. The book never uses Solomon's name, though, and many interpreters think the author takes on a Solomon-like royal role for these opening chapters, to test life at its most privileged. Verse 16, with its claim to surpass all who were over Jerusalem before, is often cited in that discussion, since only David had reigned there as Israel's king before Solomon. Others note that Jerusalem had rulers before David as well.

Ancient kings left inscriptions boasting of their buildings, wealth and wisdom, to secure a lasting name. Verse 16 sounds like that kind of royal self-praise. But verse 11 has already undercut it: no one is remembered.

A pursuit of the wind is a picture of trying to catch the wind with your hands. Verse 18 turns the value of wisdom upside down. The more the Teacher understands, the more he grieves.
passages.later: Solomon's wisdom is remembered in 1 Kings: ‘God gave Solomon wisdom, exceedingly deep insight, and understanding beyond measure, like the sand on the seashore’ (1 Kings 4:29). And Job describes the same search for wisdom: ‘But where can wisdom be found, and where does understanding dwell?’ (Job 28:12).
passages.asks: The Teacher found that knowing more made him sadder. Ask whether there is something you understand now that has made life heavier, and bring that weight to God. And ask what you have been trying to straighten that, as verse 15 says, cannot be straightened by you.
